text: You get an array nums that may contain duplicates. Return all possible unique permutations, in any order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two permutations are the same if they have the same values in the same order, no matter which copy of a value went where? So with two ones, swapping the ones does not make a new answer.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and eight, and each value is between negative ten and ten.

OK. n is at most eight, so listing every permutation is fine. The real work is not listing any of them twice. Let me run through the example. One, one, two gives only three answers, because the two ones can trade places. And one, two, three has no duplicates, so it gives all six.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to run the plain permutation backtracking and drop repeats with a set at the end. It works, but it still builds every duplicate first. I'll keep it as a checker on small inputs. This problem reminds me of backtracking with a used array, where the loop always starts at zero, combined with the sort-and-skip dedupe pattern: sort first, then skip equal values on the same level of the tree.

Here's the plan. One: sort, so equal values become neighbors. Two: in each call, loop over every unused index. Three: skip index i when it equals its left neighbor and that neighbor is not used, then mark, push, recurse, pop, unmark. One loop is one level: it picks the value for the next slot. If the left copy is not used, it was already tried in this same slot and is back off the path, so putting this copy here gives the same subtree. If the left copy is used, it sits in an earlier slot, so this copy is fine. In effect, equal values always go in left-to-right order. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The highlighted line is the dedupe. My first draft ended it with break — I'll catch that in the review. This is the final version. One thing worth flagging — the sort is a correctness requirement. The dedupe only compares neighbors, so without the sort, one, two, one gives six permutations, with duplicates. The not-used part matters too. If I only compare values and skip, one, one returns nothing at all, because the second one can never be placed.

Let's dry-run my first draft, with break, on one, one, two — expected three answers. The row that matters is back at the root: the second one equals the first, and the first is not used, so I skip. But break ends the whole loop, so two is never tried in the first slot: six calls, two answers, and two, one, one is missing. The next value is different, so it must be continue. With continue, the root goes on to two and builds two, one, one. Nine calls, all three answers. That matches.
When you search for sums over a sorted array, you can break. Why not here?

There, the break is on the sum: the array is sorted, so if the current candidate already goes over the target, every later one is at least as big and goes over too. The test is monotone for all later i, so stopping loses nothing. Here the test is same as the neighbor. That is not monotone — a later i can be a new value, like the two. So break is only safe when the condition stays true for every later i.

Let's also test with corner cases. One, two, three: both versions give all six in sixteen calls, since the line never fires — that's why the bug hides. One, one and one, one, one: one answer each, even with break. Break on two, two, one, one gives three answers instead of six. With no dedupe line, one, one gives the same answer twice. Against a brute force on all one thousand ninety-two arrays of length one to six with values one to three, continue is zero wrong and break is wrong on nine hundred forty-six.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of n times n factorial in the worst case, when all values are distinct: n factorial leaves, and each copy into the answer costs n. With duplicates, the dedupe cuts whole subtrees, so it only gets cheaper. Plus n log n for the sort. For space, the stack and used are O of n. But path is passed by value, so every level holds its own copy, which makes it O of n squared extra; passing path by reference brings it back to O of n. On one, one, two, two, three, three, four, four, with two thousand five hundred twenty answers, it takes seven thousand three hundred sixty-five calls. With no dedupe, it's one hundred nine thousand six hundred one calls.
Follow-up: some people write used of i minus one instead of not used of i minus one. Does that work? And with that version, is break OK?

Yes, it works: zero wrong on the same arrays. It forces equal values in right-to-left order instead. Oh, one more thing — with that rule, both continue and break are correct. If the left copy is on the path but this copy is not, this copy will be skipped at every deeper level too, so the path can never be finished. That node is a dead end, and breaking out of its loop loses nothing. On one, one, two, that version makes twelve calls, with three dead-end nodes. But it's slower: on the eight-element input, sixteen thousand two hundred one calls versus seven thousand three hundred sixty-five. The standard rule cuts at the top; the other one walks into dead ends first.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. Your dry run caught the break bug, and you explained it: break ends the whole loop, so the new value two is never tried. You explained when break is safe: only when the test is monotone, like a sum check on a sorted array. And you showed the used of i minus one variant, why break is fine there, and that it costs more than twice the calls. Good work.
